name: Lesotho
summary_text: Lesotho does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The common-law crime of sodomy was struck down in 2012, the US State Department's 2016 human rights report for Lesotho records no criminalisation, and a joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho likewise confirms that same-sex conduct is lawful while noting that no anti-discrimination protections exist.  There is no legal gender recognition in Lesotho. No statute permits a change of the gender marker on official documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre sets out the absence of any statutory route, and a October 2020 briefing by the same organisation with the People's Matrix Association and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho', assesses the country's law and policy against international best practice and finds no framework meeting it.  For a trans traveller the document problem is immediate. On the 2017 assessment, a person travelling on a passport whose marker does not match their presentation or stated identity could face a charge, because no statutory procedure exists to have the document recognised as consistent with the holder's gender.  The constitutional position remains an argument rather than enacted law. The 2017 analysis concludes that section 4(1) of the Constitution, through the grounds of sex and other status, should be read to cover gender identity on the authority of the UN Human Rights Committee. That interpretation has not been written into statute, and it has not been shown to have been applied by a court.  Violence and service exclusion are documented. The October 2024 joint UPR report records discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people in Lesotho, community-level discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics, and barriers to health and education services. The 2016 US State Department report separately documents societal stigma against LGBT people. Protection machinery is thin: the International Commission of Jurists' November 2024 UPR submission raised LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination as one of three key concerns for Lesotho.  Employment sits under the Labour Act 2024, which sets the current statutory framework covering unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, and forced and child labour prohibitions. The 2017 analysis records that the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omitted gender and sexual orientation.

name: Luxembourg
summary_text: Luxembourg's legal gender recognition framework rests on self-determination. The Act of 10 August 2018 replaced the previous long and costly judicial procedure with a declaration-based route to change gender status and first name(s) in the civil register, administered through the official government portal Guichet.lu. The procedure is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Recognition is binary; no nonbinary gender marker is available.  The reform was presented in May 2017 by Justice Minister Félix Braz as a bill allowing trans and intersex people to alter civil status by declaration, and it was welcomed by LGBTI associations at the time. The Chamber of Deputies approved the simplified procedure in July 2018.  Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited in employment, goods and services, education and health, with complaints handled by the CET equality body. Gender expression and sex characteristics are not named as protected grounds. The Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale provides services to LGBTI people in the country and documents this framework in its human-rights reporting.  A national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018. In July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, which organisations criticised for omitting depathologisation and other elements they consider essential.  As of 2019 reporting, Luxembourgian criminal law lacked aggravating circumstances for LGBTphobic assault, and under-reporting by victims was documented. The justice minister signalled that the law would evolve following the 2017 intervention of a European anti-discrimination monitoring body.  Prison policy is protective rather than punitive. The prison administration places detainees who disclose or openly show LGBT or trans identity so that they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations assessed case by case on the information gathered about the individual; such placements are described as exceptional. Requests by LGBT detainees to be housed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the Justice Ministry has warned against measures that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff additionally honour a detainee's chosen form of address. The planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections allowing separation by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, within those, sexual orientation. Placement therefore follows disclosed identity and need with no codified birth-sex rule, no documented special custody unit, and no solitary or administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners.  Marriage and adoption are available to same-sex couples. The country has no measures addressing conversion practices, and no measures regulating intersex medical interventions.

sources.documents: Prohibits direct and indirect discrimination based on sexual orientation and 'change of sex' (within sex) in employment, education, social security, healthcare, provision of goods and services; basis for hate-crime aggravating factor recognition
